If you are using PostgreSQL apt repository, install `postgresql-server-dev-18` and add `/usr/lib/postgresql/18/bin` to your search path. (apt uses `18, 17, 16, 15, 14, 13, 12, 11 or 10`).

If you are build PostgreSQL too, you can put **wal2json** directory inside contrib, change the contrib Makefile (variable SUBDIRS) and build it following the Installation from Source Code on Windows instructions. * Apache webserver with mod_rewrite and .htaccess file support enabled
* PHP 5 with PDO and SQLite driver enabled
* **cms/data** - directory of the SQLite database files, needs to be writable by the webserver
* **content.sqlite**, **entries.sqlite** and **userdata.sqlite** - SQLite database files, need to be writable by the webserver
* **cms/cache** - cache directory, needs to be writable if you want to use the caching feature
* **cms/media** and **cms/files** - need to be writable if you want to use the file uploader

The server hands its own usage guide to every agent that connects, so there's no instructions file to copy around. The quick start covers the rest.
- **Skills**: SKILL.md documents compiled from your experience in a domain, so the agent works your way from the first prompt. Nothing changes without your say-so. See the skill compiler.

- **Hooks for Claude Code**: memory that works without the agent choosing to use it, because mostly it doesn't. `omnimem hook` puts the project's briefing in the opening context of every session, stops a tool call that repeats a known dead end before it runs (handing back what failed and what worked instead), and records what a session changed when it ends. `omnimem install-hooks` sets them up. Over ten paired runs on one task, every attempt at the abandoned approach was stopped, no treated run hit a failing test suite against 8 of 10 without, and it cost 27% less.
- **The graveyard**: every dead end is logged with what you tried, why it failed and how long it cost you. The agent checks it before suggesting a library or pattern.
- **Experience scoring**: something that took four attempts and a weird workaround to crack is gold. The harder it was, the more readily it comes back.
- **Memory lifecycle**: `ACTIVE → DEPRIORITISED → ARCHIVED → DELETED`. "Forget about X" usually means stop bringing it up, not wipe it from existence.
- **Contradiction detection**: a quick check on every write, and a deeper look with Claude Haiku when you want one.
- **Semantic deduplication**: near-duplicates get flagged as they're written and cleaned up in bulk with `find_duplicates()`.
- **One-call briefing**: `briefing()` hands over project context, experience stats, stale memories, new articles, contradictions and skill suggestions in one go.
- **The skill compiler**: turns reinforced lessons and dead ends into loadable skills, behind a propose-and-accept gate so a one-off opinion can't quietly become policy.
- **Auto-maintenance**: duplicates archived, contradictions flagged, expired articles tidied, all in the background.
- **Licence and provenance**: every memory records whether it can be redistributed and who's speaking (you, the agent, or a source it retrieved), so a later session can tell evidence from inference.

- **Trust**: whether OmniMem believes a memory, not just whether it shows it. A fact it extracted for itself waits for you to confirm it, one side of a confirmed contradiction is marked disputed, a memory a newer one replaced folds into it, and one you've judged wrong never comes back. Only you can confirm or reject, in the settings window or the terminal, never an agent.

Write your schema and business logic as a **module** in Rust, C#, TypeScript, or C++. SpacetimeDB compiles it, runs it inside the database, and automatically synchronizes state to connected clients in real-time.
SpacetimeDB application architecture (elements in white are provided by SpacetimeDB)

SpacetimeDB is optimized for maximum speed and minimum latency. SpacetimeDB provides all the ACID guarantees of a traditional RDBMS, with all the speed of an optimized web server. Hot data stays in memory for fast access and colder data lives on disk, while a commit log provides durability and crash recovery. The entire backend of our MMORPG BitCraft Online runs as a single SpacetimeDB module: chat, items, terrain, player positions, everything, synchronized to thousands of players in real-time.
That is it. This creates a project from a template, publishes it to Maincloud, and watches for file changes, automatically rebuilding and republishing on save. See pricing for details.

SpacetimeDB is well suited to web application backends, from everyday CRUD apps to reactive ones like collaborative tools, live dashboards, and chat. Write your module in TypeScript and connect from the browser with the TypeScript SDK, which includes React hooks like `useTable` and integrations for Vue, Svelte, Angular, and other frameworks. Each reducer runs as an ACID transaction, and subscribed clients receive committed changes automatically, so you don't need polling, a separate API server, or a pub/sub layer to keep them in sync. The `chat-react-ts` template from the Quick Start is a working example.

Every transaction that changes data is written to an on-disk commitlog, which is replayed to recover the database after a crash. Transactions are fsynced in batches, so many transactions share a single `fsync` (group commit) (`local.rs`).

Since SpacetimeDB 2.0, clients get confirmed reads by default: the server holds back a transaction's subscription updates, and the caller's reducer result, until that transaction is durable (`client_connection.rs`), so the data a client receives from its subscriptions and reducer calls will survive a crash. SQL queries over HTTP wait for durability by default too. On Maincloud and other replicated deployments, durable instead means persisted by the replicas the database's replication settings require. Apps that can tolerate a client occasionally seeing a write that is then lost in a crash, like many games, can opt out with `withConfirmedReads(false)` for lower latency.

`okapi-core` has no framework dependencies, so any JVM service can use it, from a Ktor app to a background worker. You assemble the pieces yourself — create the store, the deliverer, and the processor, start an `OutboxScheduler`, and hand it a `TransactionRunner` (a one-method interface wrapping a block in whatever transaction mechanism you already use). - **PostgreSQL:** 001 table and initial indexes, 002 route-aware claim index, 003 `TIMESTAMPTZ` timestamp columns, 004 retry backoff column and claim index (its second changeset must run outside a transaction)
- **MySQL:** 001 table and initial indexes, 002 route-aware claim index, 003 `DATETIME(6)` timestamp columns, 004 retry backoff column and claim index

PostgreSQL's `003` converts the timestamp columns from `TIMESTAMP` (the okapi JVM's local wall-clock time) to `TIMESTAMPTZ`. It reads existing values in the session `TimeZone`; pgjdbc sets that to the JVM default zone, so the bundled Liquibase changelog converts them correctly when it runs inside the application. When applying it by hand, run it inside a transaction (`psql -1`) after `SET TIME ZONE '<zone your okapi JVMs run in>'` in the same session. It takes an `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` lock: it first waits (up to 30 s, then fails and retries on the next start) for open transactions on `okapi_outbox`, queuing every other statement on the table meanwhile, and then, unless the session zone is UTC (PostgreSQL 12+), rewrites the table while reads and writes wait. 1.x instances keep working after it, apart from one failed poll per pooled connection. See UPGRADING.md for when the in-app conversion uses the wrong zone. See UPGRADING.md.

MySQL's `003` converts the timestamp columns from `TIMESTAMP(6)`, which ends in January 2038, to `DATETIME(6)` holding UTC. Stop every 1.x instance, publishers included, before it runs: 1.x writes these columns in the JVM zone. It copies the table; it first waits (up to 30 s, then fails and retries on the next start) for open transactions on `okapi_outbox` to finish, queuing every other statement on the table meanwhile, and then blocks writes, including `publish()`, until the copy finishes. See UPGRADING.md, including when rows written by 1.x can read back shifted.

Knowledge graph as a make-sense layer

GLiNER extracts entities from every memory and document chunk at ingestion time and links them to the graph automatically. But automatic extraction alone generates noise. EcoDB combines GLiNER with an **entity dictionary**, a curated list of allowed entities with canonical names and aliases. Dictionary matches take priority over raw NER predictions. Entities that don't match the dictionary are flagged as candidates for human review.
